questions.q: Why isn't raw reconnaissance output (WHOIS data, a Shodan result set, Nmap scans, theHarvester exports) enough on its own?
options: Raw tool output is always inaccurate and must be discarded
It's scattered across separate tool outputs with no consistent structure, so nobody can answer "what's our actual attack surface?" from it directly
Tool output can never be used in a professional report
Only Nmap output is considered valid evidence in a real engagement
questions.explain: Each tool produces its own output format in isolation; the attack surface map is the single structured artifact that consolidates all of it into something a team can actually act on.

questions.q: Besides the asset itself, what two fields does a real attack surface map entry need that a bare IP list doesn't provide?
options: The asset's physical GPS coordinates and the tester's home address
The source the finding came from and the open ports/services discovered for it
The target company's annual revenue and stock ticker
The tester's personal opinion of the company's leadership
questions.explain: A usable map ties each asset to where it was discovered (source) and what's actually open or exposed on it — the fields that make the finding actionable and traceable.

questions.q: Why tag findings as confirmed, probable, or unconfirmed rather than treating every entry the same?
options: So a verified open port isn't given the same weight as a lead that still needs corroboration, like a job posting implying a technology
Confidence tagging is only cosmetic and has no effect on prioritization
Because unconfirmed findings must always be deleted from the map
Because only confirmed findings are allowed to appear in the final report
questions.explain: A subdomain confirmed by both crt.sh and a live Nmap scan deserves more weight than an implication from a single job posting; tagging keeps the team from treating a guess as a verified fact.

questions.q: How does the attack surface map connect directly into Chapter 3's scanning and enumeration work?
options: It replaces the need for any further scanning entirely
It is discarded once the recon phase ends and rebuilt from scratch later
It only matters for the final report, not for any technical next step
Every host and port already identified in the map becomes the input list for deeper service and version enumeration
questions.explain: Rather than re-discovering the same hosts, Chapter 3 starts from exactly what the map already contains, using it as the handoff artifact between reconnaissance and deeper enumeration.

questions.q: If an asset turns up during recon that was never named in the signed Rules of Engagement, what should happen according to the lesson?
options: Quietly add it to the map and continue testing it like any in-scope asset
Ignore it completely and delete any record that it was found
It becomes a conversation with the client before anything else touches it, rather than something quietly included
Scan it immediately to determine if it's worth including
questions.explain: A structured map makes scope compliance checkable at a glance; an out-of-scope asset needs client clarification before any further action, matching the authorization discipline from earlier lessons.
